title: Network Installation, Security, and Recovery

sources.title: FBLA Network Design 2026-27 Guidelines, study guide p. 6
sources.scope: Read the current study-guide objective descriptions for installation/configuration and network security/recovery; establishes scope, not mechanisms.

sources.title: Cisco: Configure IP Access Lists
sources.scope: Read ACL matching, ordered evaluation, implicit deny, direction/application, traffic criteria, and stateful inspection discussion. Platform-specific examples; not a universal firewall configuration recipe.

sources.title: RFC 3021: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links
sources.scope: Read sections 1-3 and deployment notes: /31 uses both addresses as hosts only on point-to-point links; both endpoints must support it.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: BitLocker Overview
sources.scope: Read volume-encryption purpose, TPM/offline integrity role, startup protection, and recovery-key backup behavior; warns encryption without protected keys is insufficient.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Active Directory Domain Services overview
sources.scope: Read directory objects, centralized account access, authentication, access control, policy administration, and replication. Distinguishes directory function from DNS naming.

sources.title: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9: Using SELinux
sources.scope: Read guide introduction: SELinux implements MAC; policy constrains how users/processes interact with files and devices. Platform-specific Linux control, not antivirus.

sources.title: CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model
sources.scope: Read current model overview: per-request least-privilege decisions, location-centric to data-centric shift, visibility and granular enforcement.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Print and Document Services Architecture
sources.scope: Read print queue, client/server sharing, driver and spooler architecture. Windows Server 2012-era source; used only for durable queue/host dependency concepts, not current driver deployment advice.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide
sources.scope: Read publication overview and planning purpose/process metadata. Detailed operational claims below are kept to general plan, backup, recovery-test concepts; document is 2010 guidance, not current vendor prescription.

sources.title: Cisco: What Is Ethernet?
sources.scope: Read Ethernet/IEEE 802.3, frame switching and MAC learning versus router IP forwarding, and physical media overview; not used for universal cable reach.

sources.title: IEEE 802.11 Working Group and amendments
sources.scope: Verified IEEE 802.11 is the Wireless LAN Working Group standard family; IEEE-SA amendment pages identify 802.11ax-2021 and 802.11be-2024. No universal device rate or range inferred.

pages.title: SOHO edge and traffic controls
notes: A modem terminates an ISP access link; an ONT serves fiber.
A router forwards IP packets between distinct networks.
A switch forwards LAN frames using learned MAC addresses.
A SOHO gateway may combine router, switch, AP and firewall.
DHCP leases addresses and options such as gateway and DNS.
DNS resolves names; it does not assign a host its address.
NAT rewrites address or port fields between address realms.
NAT is not a firewall rule or a security guarantee.
Place an edge firewall to enforce permitted traffic flows.

pages.title: Firewall rules and ACL behavior
notes: A hardware firewall is a dedicated appliance or function.
A software firewall filters traffic on a host or gateway.
An ACL matches fields such as direction, IP, protocol, port.
Ordered rules evaluate until a match; order changes outcome.
Cisco IOS ACLs have implicit deny after listed entries.
A rule has no effect until applied at an interface or policy.
Stateful inspection tracks sessions for return traffic.
Allow only required flows; close unused services and ports.
Test intended and denied traffic; narrow rules limit exposure.
ACL syntax and default behavior vary by product and context.

pages.title: Wireless setup and physical media
notes: An AP bridges 802.11 clients to a LAN; a router routes.
A gateway joins networks; default gateway is off-subnet hop.
Twisted pairs reduce interference; shielding adds protection.
Ethernet rate and reach depend on specified PHY and cable.
Fiber uses light; mode, optics, wavelength and loss set reach.
LC connector shape alone cannot establish fiber compatibility.
802.11ax/be are WLAN amendments; bands vary.
RF range varies with walls, interference, band and antennas.
PHY headline rate is not application throughput or a promise.

pages.title: Subnet masks and loopback
notes: IPv4 prefix counts contiguous network bits in the mask.
A /24 mask is 255.255.255.0; do not infer from old classes.
Address AND mask yields network; aligned blocks avoid overlap.
Ordinary LAN subnet reserves network and broadcast addresses.
RFC 3021 uses both /31 addresses as point-to-point hosts.
Both ends must support /31; not a usual multi-host LAN.
IPv4 127.0.0.1 loopback tests this host, not a remote path.
Connect modem/ONT to WAN; set LAN, DHCP, unique admin secret.
Use WPA3 or WPA2-AES; avoid WEP and weak passphrases.

practice.prompt: A PC has a valid LAN address but cannot reach an off-subnet server. Which SOHO settings and devices would you check first, and why?
practice.answer: Check mask, DHCP-provided default gateway, router WAN/ISP handoff, then name resolution separately. The router forwards off-subnet traffic; DNS only resolves names. Integrated gateways may combine modem, router and AP roles.

practice.prompt: Why can a permit ACL above a deny rule change results, and when is /31 appropriate?
practice.answer: Cisco IOS ACLs evaluate in order to first match, then implicit deny applies if none match. /31 uses its two addresses as hosts only on a point-to-point link whose endpoints support it, not a normal shared LAN.

pages.title: Fiber and copper selection
notes: Copper Ethernet sends signals over twisted pairs.
UTP lacks metallic shielding; STP includes shielding.
Shield installation and grounding must follow cable design.
Cable category, endpoints and PHY constrain rate and channel.
Coax has a central conductor and shield; some ISPs use it.
Fiber carries light and resists electromagnetic interference.
Multimode commonly serves shorter links with matching optics.
Single-mode with compatible optics can serve longer links.
Reach depends on PHY, optics, wavelength, loss and connectors.

pages.title: Rack and blade installation
notes: Rack servers mount as units in a cabinet with service access.
Check rail fit, equipment depth, weight and rack capacity.
Plan labeled power, network ports, cable paths and airflow.
Blade servers fit a shared chassis with common interconnects.
Chassis can improve density and centralized management.
Chassis adds cost and shared failure dependencies.
Inventory assets, firmware, NICs, storage and switch ports.
Follow vendor install, grounding and safety procedures.
After install, verify links, management, alarms and logs.
Redundant PSUs help only with adequate independent feeds.

pages.title: Power, temperature, and UPS
notes: Excess heat can throttle equipment, age it or shut it down.
Keep vents clear; monitor inlet temperature and airflow.
Cooling capacity and airflow must suit the installed load.
A UPS supplies temporary battery power during an interruption.
Size runtime to load; test batteries and controlled shutdown.
A UPS is not a generator, backup, or independent power feed.
Power redundancy fails if upstream circuits share one failure.
Define recovery priorities and dependencies before controls.
Tabletop power loss; predict effects; do not unplug live gear.

pages.title: Direct, shared, and server printing
notes: Direct USB printing connects a client to one printer.
A network printer can accept jobs directly over the LAN.
Host-shared printing exposes a host queue to other clients.
The host and its print service must stay available for jobs.
A print server centralizes queues and printer administration.
Clients submit jobs to a queue; spooler manages pending work.
A server outage or queue fault can interrupt shared printing.
Restrict queue management and printing to authorized users.
Keep printer firmware and drivers supported and maintained.
Protect confidential output; use secure release if available.

practice.prompt: An office has 40 users, two printers, and rotating staff. Compare a host-shared printer with a print server.
practice.answer: Host sharing is simple but jobs depend on that host's uptime and controls. A print server can centrally manage queues and permissions, but introduces a service to maintain and secure; choose based on support and availability needs.

practice.prompt: Why does a blade chassis improve density but not automatically improve resilience?
practice.answer: Blades share chassis infrastructure such as power, cooling and interconnects, increasing density and management convenience while creating common failure dependencies. Validate independent feeds and capacity; redundancy labels alone do not prove independence.

pages.title: Threat defenses and least privilege
notes: DoS exhausts a service resource; DDoS distributes that load.
Capacity, filtering and provider aid may mitigate DoS.
Phishing deceives users into disclosing data or taking action.
Verify requests via known channels; report suspicious mail.
Insider risk may be intentional or accidental.
Least privilege limits access to needed tasks and time.
Remove unused services; close ports and patch systems.
Antivirus detects some threats; it cannot assure safety.
Third-party access needs scope, oversight and revocation.

pages.title: Zero Trust and network admission
notes: Zero Trust grants no automatic trust merely from LAN location.
Evaluate each access request using identity and context.
Grant granular least-privilege access to data and services.
Reassess decisions as users, devices and risk context change.
MFA combines factor types; two passwords are one type.
Authentication checks identity; authorization grants actions.
NAC checks device or identity at network admission.
NAC may quarantine a device pending remediation or compliance.
VLAN segmentation needs policy controls on inter-VLAN traffic.
NAC complements endpoint, identity controls and monitoring.

pages.title: BitLocker and directory identity
notes: BitLocker encrypts Windows volumes against offline exposure.
TPM can protect startup keys and check offline integrity.
Startup PIN or key can add preboot access protection.
Encryption does not protect data in an open session.
Protect and back up recovery keys for legitimate recovery.
AD DS stores directory objects such as accounts and groups.
Domain identity centralizes authentication and access control.
Policy-based administration manages settings across systems.
DNS locates services; a DNS name is not AD identity.

pages.title: SELinux mandatory access control
notes: SELinux is Linux Security-Enhanced Linux access control.
It implements mandatory access control (MAC) through policy.
Policy constrains user and process interaction with objects.
File and process labels provide context for policy decisions.
Rules can restrict services beyond ordinary file permissions.
This can limit damage if a process is compromised.
Investigate denials; fix policy, do not blindly disable it.
SELinux is not antivirus; updates and backups still matter.
MAC policy differs from discretionary owner/group permissions.
Use platform docs for modes and safe policy administration.

practice.prompt: A compliant school laptop connects to a guest VLAN but cannot reach an internal file server. Explain a Zero Trust/NAC design reason.
practice.answer: NAC may admit the device only to a restricted segment; authorization can still deny the file-server resource. Verify identity, posture and the specific permitted flow rather than assuming LAN presence grants trust.

practice.prompt: Contrast BitLocker, AD DS, and SELinux; which one is a volume-encryption feature?
practice.answer: BitLocker encrypts Windows volumes to reduce offline exposure; AD DS centrally stores identities and administers authentication/access; SELinux applies Linux MAC policy to process/object interactions. None alone replaces layered controls.

pages.title: Disaster recovery planning
notes: Disaster recovery restores systems and data after disruption.
Business continuity sustains priority work during disruption.
A plan defines scope, roles, contacts and dependencies.
Include recovery order, communication, resources and checks.
Risk assessment compares events and business impacts.
Recovery time objective (RTO) is target restoration time.
Recovery point objective (RPO) is tolerable data-loss time.
Select controls to meet business targets and resource limits.
Test plans; revise after exercises, incidents or changes.

pages.title: Backup types and restore assurance
notes: Cloud backup is offsite but depends on provider and account.
NAS backup is convenient but shares site and access risks.
External drives can be disconnected; rotate them securely.
Use 3-2-1: three copies, two media, one copy offsite.
Keep an offline or immutable copy to resist ransomware.
Versioned copies allow selection of an earlier restore point.
Separate backup credentials from admin accounts.
RAID may sustain disk failure, not deletion or corruption.
A backup is an independent copy; RAID is not a backup.
Test isolated restores; validate data, rights and service.

pages.title: IDS, IPS, updates, and response
notes: An IDS observes host or network activity and raises alerts.
An IPS can block or drop traffic inline when policy triggers.
Inline false positives may disrupt legitimate service.
Detection depends on visibility, tuning and known indicators.
An alert is a lead to investigate, not proof of compromise.
Preserve evidence, contain, remediate, then validate recovery.
Patch supported systems and apps to fix known flaws.
Test updates and plan rollback; delay prolongs exposure.
Firewalls and endpoint protection work at different points.

pages.title: Wireless authentication and ACLs
notes: WPA2/WPA3 protect Wi-Fi links; choose supported secure modes.
WPA2-Personal uses shared passphrase; protect it if exposed.
Enterprise Wi-Fi can use 802.1X/EAP user or device identity.
A backend validates credentials; protect its server and keys.
Use a unique secret, current firmware and secure admin access.
WPA3 compatibility depends on AP and client support.
Wireless ACLs filter traffic by rules and attributes.
MAC addresses can be spoofed; ACLs are not identity proof.
Isolate guest clients and restrict paths with network policy.
Revoke lost credentials; hidden SSID is not security.

practice.prompt: A ransomware scenario has a recent encrypted NAS copy and a week-old offline copy. Which restore choice should the team investigate?
practice.answer: Investigate the offline version as a potentially cleaner restore point, while validating age against the RPO and checking integrity in an isolated environment. NAS proximity alone does not make it safe; RAID and online copies may share compromise.

practice.prompt: An IPS blocked a legitimate file-transfer flow. What differs from IDS behavior, and what should operators do?
practice.answer: IDS primarily detects and alerts; IPS can enforce a block inline, so a false positive can interrupt service. Review evidence and rule scope, safely tune with change control, then validate both desired and prohibited flows.

lab.title: Offline network and recovery tabletop
steps: Draw a fictional ISP-to-SOHO path and label modem, router, switch, AP, DHCP, DNS and firewall roles.
On paper, evaluate ordered allow/deny rules and identify an unintended flow; make no device changes.
Use a sample subnet card to find network and gateway; explain why /31 is point-to-point only.
Sort fictional backup copies by location, medium and version; select a restore candidate against stated RTO/RPO.
For a mock access request, decide NAC admission and Zero Trust authorization separately.
Review sample IDS/IPS alert cards and state what evidence is needed before declaring an incident.
expected: Learner distinguishes NAT, routing, DHCP/DNS, ACL policy and stateful filtering.
Learner explains fiber/copper/WLAN limits and accurate subnet/loopback purposes.
Learner compares direct/shared/server printing and rack/blade power dependencies.
Learner selects a tested, versioned restore approach and explains RAID is not backup.
Learner distinguishes BitLocker encryption, AD DS identity/policy and SELinux MAC.
Learner explains IDS alert versus IPS inline blocking and WPA/ACL limits.

limitations: Cisco ACL behavior cited is IOS-specific; other firewall products can differ in rule order, defaults and state handling.
Microsoft print architecture reference describes Windows Server 2012; queue and host dependency concepts are used, not current driver deployment instructions.
Fiber reach and exact PHY rates require the actual cable, optics, standard and vendor specifications; no universal distance/rate is asserted.
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 is older guidance; organization-specific recovery requirements and current policy govern implementation.
